rv.q: Graham has masterfully brought home the debt we surely owe to Keynes, and in so doing has once again raised the overall standard of our national theatrical life.
The dialogue is both deftly intelligent and blissfully funny, hence the comparison with Stoppard.
The subtlety in Graham’s so approachable play is in suggesting a congruence between Keynes’s economics and Lopokova’s art.
The dismal science of economics has rarely been more colourful.
What is most remarkable is that what might sound like a very dry subject is delivered by Kinnear as a fascinating, fun-filled and even frolicsome evening.
James Graham’s high-wire writing brings economic theory to life and connects it with art and fulfilment in this polished, ravishingly staged story of John Maynard Keynes.
The Standard of Living will prove to be anything but dry, rolling through the momentous events and multiple crises of the early 20th century.
It is, to be fair, almost certainly the most enjoyable play about an economist ever written.
Graham hasn’t found the form to turn so much content into a drama with a compelling hook.
This is a play of ideas, but unlike Tom Stoppard’s brilliant, recently revived Arcadia, it can’t turn the abstract territory of maths and logic into something richly emotive.
It’s irredeemably dry and ultimately, I’m genuinely sorry to say, a colossal yawn.

Graham has managed to elevate a mere sequence of historical milestones into something far more engaging and playful, brought to life by a terrific ensemble and a confident and astute central performance from the ever-watchable Kinnear.
This major West End premiere presents the life of John Maynard Keynes to audiences in a captivating night of theatre, bringing one of the 20th century’s most influential thought leaders to the stage.
This is art about the importance of art and is both uplifting and hopeful.
Yet despite Graham's adept writing, there is too much ground to cover in the space of the play.
The Standard of Living has good intentions but doesn’t heed its own final call to ‘act.’

It is hard to imagine a better tribute to the Keynes who, in irritated exile in Cambridge, founded its first ever theatre and whose last great triumph, with WW2 still to pay for, was to enthuse the 1945 government to found not only the NHS but the Arts Council.
By bringing Keynes into the West End, Graham and Hytner have created a production that is intellectually ambitious yet theatrically spectacular in every sense.
Nicholas Hytner’s production is commendably fluid and engaging.
Graham achieves this by pitting Keynes against his real rival and antithesis, Friedrich Hayek, in a series of miniature debates.
The Standard of Living is incredibly engaging and educational, but Graham tries to accomplish a little too much.
Nicholas Hytner’s epic production of this epic play has a confident sweep that is often a joy to watch.
Graham's intelligent drama interweaves the personal and political to great effect, though in covering so many bases, nuance is occasionally lost.
Still an enjoyable albeit an unremarkable watch, it is worth seeing if only for the fantastic performances from the cast, all of which take this disappointingly uneven play up to a higher standard.

Yet the conflict of economic theory never – and surely never can – achieve the hair-raising drama of, say, Hytner’s previous production Giant, the hit Mark Rosenblatt play that excavated Roald Dahl’s antisemitism.
It's a satisfying and enlightening night of theatre.
Such an interweaving of big and little ideas is gripping.
For the most part, it succeeds, finding wit and humanity within some very big ideas.
Ultimately, this portrait of a life seemingly ill-suited for broad-brush theatre makes easy work of the task against the odds.

The Standard Of Living is an interesting evening in the company of a man whose story may have some influence over the way we live our lives today but is probably more for James Graham die-hard fans only rather than a mainstream audience.

Despite some witty inclusions from acclaimed writer James Graham’s script, along with a creative blend of dance and dialogue, The Standard of Living struggles to get its sums right in this biographical work.
The Standard of Living is an interesting rather than consistently compelling play, but there is plenty to admire in its ambition, intelligent writing and strong performances.

cn.t: Critics are divided on Graham's ambitious Keynes biography: some praise Kinnear's charm and the play's intellectual scope, while others find it overstuffed and dull, struggling to balance economics, art, and personal life into compelling drama.
